query: For single-phase ZrB2 ceramic, which requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and may lack the strength and structural integrity needed for service, what single intervention could lower the required preparation temperature and reduce the holes and eventual component failure caused by prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention and its mechanism, predict its performance compared with conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2, define the relevant preparation and service boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and describe a controlled preparation, integrity, and long-duration exposure experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Field-assisted spark-plasma sintering (SPS) of commercial ZrB₂ powder at 50 MPa and 1900 °C for 10 min will (a) densify the ceramic to ≥ 98 % of theoretical density—about 6 percentage points higher than conventional hot-pressing at 2300 °C—and (b) cut the number of through-thickness pores that act as initiation sites for liquid-bath attack by at least 50 %.  As a result, after 500 h immersion in a 60 °C acidic Ni-plating bath the SPS material will retain ≥ 90 % of its initial four-point-bend strength, compared with ≤ 60 % retention for the conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB₂.
generation.material_initial_state: Commercial –325-mesh ZrB₂ powder (2–5 µm mean size) containing the typical ~0.5 wt % B₂O₃ surface layer; no deliberate second phases or sintering additives.
generation.intervention: Spark-plasma sintering (pulsed d.c., 100 °C min⁻¹ ramp) to 1900 °C under 50 MPa uniaxial pressure for 10 min in flowing Ar, followed by furnace cooling.
generation.conditions: Preparation in graphite die, base pressure <10 Pa before back-filling with Ar; service test in continuously stirred NiSO₄–H₃BO₃–HCl (Watts) plating bath at 60 °C and pH 4.0.
generation.structural_mediator: Rapid Joule heating and local plasma cleaning at particle contacts remove the native B₂O₃ film and generate short-lived liquid Zr–B droplets, enhancing grain-boundary diffusion so densification proceeds at ≈ 400 °C lower temperature, producing a finer-grained (> 95 % <3 µm), near-pore-free microstructure.
generation.mechanism: Lower porosity and smaller, more tortuous residual pores impede capillary penetration of plating solution; the absence of large surface-connected voids limits localized dissolution of ZrB₂, thereby delaying hole growth and crack coalescence that otherwise cause premature component failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative density ≥ 98 % (versus 92 ± 2 % conventional); room-temperature four-point-bend strength 550–600 MPa (versus 400–450 MPa); after 500 h plating-bath exposure the SPS sample keeps ≥ 90 % of its initial strength and shows ≤ 3 surface-breaking voids mm⁻², whereas the baseline shows ≥ 8 voids mm⁻² and strength loss to ≤ 60 %.
generation.baseline: Hot-pressed single-phase ZrB₂ prepared from the same powder at 2300 °C, 30 MPa, 1 h hold in Ar.
generation.boundary: Valid for ZrB₂ powders with particle size ≤5 µm, SPS loads 30–60 MPa, peak temperature 1800–2000 °C, and liquid-bath service temperatures ≤120 °C.  Results may not extrapolate to coarser powders, atmospheric-pressure sintering, or molten-salt / >120 °C corrosion environments.
generation.uncertainty: Scale-up to parts thicker than 15 mm may produce temperature gradients that lower density; variations in residual oxygen or carbon could change densification kinetics; long-term (>1000 h) bath chemistry drift has not been assessed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches (n = 6 bars each, 3 × 4 × 45 mm) from the same powder: (A) SPS under the stated conditions; (B) conventional hot-press baseline.  Measure density (Archimedes) and initial four-point-bend strength.  Immerse half of each batch for 500 h in a 60 °C Watts bath while keeping the other half dry as mechanical controls.  After exposure, measure strength again and quantify surface-breaking pores by SEM image analysis at 500× on polished cross-sections.
measurements: Four-point-bend strength (MPa) before and after exposure
Cross-sectional SEM micrographs for grain size and pore morphology
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if either (i) SPS samples fail to reach ≥ 96 % density OR show post-bath strength retention < 75 %, OR (ii) pore density reduction is < 25 % relative to baseline.
